analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and legal remedies for employers who pay women less than men for equal work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Labor Committee for two years and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strengthen the laws against paying women less than men for jobs requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility. It would make it illegal for employers to punish workers for discussing their wages, add compensatory and punitive damages for equal-pay violations, allow those cases to proceed as class actions, require large employers to report pay data by race, sex, and national origin to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and fund federal research, training, and a voluntary program recognizing employers who fix pay gaps. It was introduced in January 1997 and referred to the Senate Labor Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Working women who are paid less than men for comparable work, and their families, who would gain stronger tools to challenge unequal pay: easier class-action suits, punitive and compensatory damages, protection against retaliation for discussing wages, and federal studies and training aimed at closing pay gaps. Workers at employers with 100 or more employees would also benefit from required pay-data reporting that would expose disparities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women facing pay discrimination and their families

how_it_helps.text: Adds a nonretaliation rule to the Fair Labor Standards Act so employers cannot punish employees who inquire about, discuss, or disclose wages, making it easier for workers to learn when they are being underpaid.

Makes employers who violate equal-pay requirements liable for compensatory or punitive damages, beyond the back-pay now recoverable, and allows equal-pay cases to be maintained as class actions, including recovery of expert fees.
Authorizes the Secretary of Labor to seek additional compensatory or punitive damages in equal-pay enforcement cases, giving the government a stronger deterrent tool.
Directs the EEOC to require employers with 100 or more employees to report pay information analyzed by race, sex, and national origin, giving regulators and workers data on where disparities exist.

Funds training, research, and a national summit on eliminating pay disparities, and creates a voluntary program of federal guidelines and an award recognizing employers who adjust wage scales so women are paid fairly.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially large ones, would bear new costs: exposure to compensatory and punitive damages and class-action lawsuits over equal-pay violations, new payroll-record and pay-data reporting requirements for firms with 100 or more employees, and compliance work under federal guidelines.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers facing damages and reporting

drawbacks.text: Expanding remedies to punitive damages and class actions would increase litigation against employers, including meritless suits, raising legal costs for businesses of all sizes that must defend wage comparisons.

Requiring employers with 100 or more workers to keep payroll records and report pay data analyzed by race, sex, and national origin would create new administrative burdens, a concern the bill itself acknowledges by instructing the President to minimize burdens on reporting entities.

Requiring employers to compare pay across different job categories rests on judgments about which jobs are 'equivalent,' which can be contested and could push employers toward rigid pay structures rather than market-based ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core is strengthening enforcement of an existing legal right — equal pay for equal work — through damages, class actions, retaliation protection, and pay transparency, while leaving pay scales themselves to employers. The real costs fall on employers in litigation exposure and reporting, and the pay-data requirement would have made disparities easier to prove. The bill was drawn with soft edges — voluntary evaluation guidelines, employer recognition awards, and a directive to minimize reporting burdens — so the main trade-off is stronger worker remedies versus higher compliance and litigation costs for business.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee in January 1997, and the committee never reported it out, so it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle and ten other Democratic senators introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act on January 21, 1997.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day it was introduced.

Over the next two years the only actions were a star print ordered in March 1998 and the sponsor's introductory remarks in June 1998; the committee never held it, and no version ever reached the Senate floor.
Twenty-three senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill.
The bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, particularly large ones, avoided the bill's new damages exposure, class-action liability, and pay-data reporting requirements, since the rules were never enacted. Women seeking stronger equal-pay enforcement gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers, which avoided new penalties

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act on January 21, 1997, with ten Democratic colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: 23 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Mikulski, Murray, Kerry, Leahy, Reid, Boxer, Harkin, and Wyden.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in January 1997 and never reported it out; no hearing or markup appears in the record in two years.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to sit in committee for the full two-year Congress without a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat — 23 senators plus sponsor Daschle — and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and chairing the Labor Committee, the bill had no path to a vote.

industries.note: They would face punitive and compensatory damages, class-action equal-pay suits, and mandatory pay-data reporting to the EEOC. Industry's interest in stopping the bill ran against workers' ability to enforce equal pay, and stopping it succeeded.
Class-action equal-pay cases with expert fees and expanded damages would create new work for lawyers representing workers. Their gain comes directly from workers' stronger remedies.
New recordkeeping and pay-data reporting requirements for large employers would generate compliance work. The cost to employers is a burden; the data gathered serves enforcement.
